messages.content: Explain all seven rules of this fictional queue, and why each matters. Facts: capacity is 100 jobs; jobs beyond capacity are rejected rather than silently dropped; a running job has a 30-second lease; workers renew the lease every 10 seconds; an expired lease makes the job available again; handlers must be idempotent because a job can run twice; only explicit acknowledgement removes a job. Explain the relationship between renewal, expiry, duplicate runs, and acknowledgement. Also, a separate dashboard color change is planned, but that is irrelevant here.

acceptance.answerPlacement: Opens with a substantive explanation of queue behavior, without announcing the explanation.
acceptance.actionableSteps: Explains the renewal/expiry/idempotency/acknowledgement relationship usefully; does not invent operational tasks.
acceptance.completeness: Covers all seven facts and why each matters, with no dashboard tangent or invented exactly-once guarantee.

responses.text:
The queue uses renewable leases to make abandoned jobs available again. Because a job can run twice, handlers must be idempotent; only explicit acknowledgement removes a job.

Capacity and execution:

1. **Capacity is 100 jobs.** This defines the queue’s limit.
2. **Jobs beyond capacity are rejected.** They are not silently dropped, so exceeding the limit produces an explicit rejection.
3. **A running job has a 30-second lease.** Its claim on the job is time-limited.
4. **Workers renew the lease every 10 seconds.** Renewal keeps the claim active while the worker runs the job; without renewal, the lease can expire.

Recovery and removal:

5. **An expired lease makes the job available again.** This allows another execution when the previous lease is no longer active. Expiry makes the job available; it does not remove it.
6. **Handlers must be idempotent because a job can run twice.** Repeating the job must not produce unintended additional effects. Lease expiry can make a previously running job available for another run.
7. **Only explicit acknowledgement removes a job.** Renewal maintains the lease, and expiry makes the job available again. Neither removes it; acknowledgement is the removal operation.

responses.text:
The queue retains a job until explicit acknowledgement; a lease controls when another worker can take it.

1. **Capacity is 100 jobs.** This sets the queue’s limit.
2. **Jobs beyond capacity are rejected.** Rejection makes the capacity failure visible instead of silently losing jobs.
3. **A running job has a 30-second lease.** The lease limits how long a worker can hold a job without renewal.
4. **Workers renew every 10 seconds.** Renewal keeps the lease active while work continues, with renewals scheduled more frequently than the 30-second lease duration.
5. **An expired lease makes the job available again.** Expiry lets another worker take a job whose lease was not maintained. It does not remove the job.
6. **Handlers must be idempotent because a job can run twice.** Repeating a job must not produce additional unintended effects. Lease expiry and reassignment can lead to a second run even if the first run already did work.
7. **Only explicit acknowledgement removes a job.** Renewal maintains the lease, and expiry makes the job available again; neither removes it. Completing the handler’s work without acknowledgement leaves the job subject to another run after lease expiry.

messages.content: Explain all seven rules of this fictional queue, and why each matters. Facts: capacity is 100 jobs; jobs beyond capacity are rejected rather than silently dropped; a running job has a 30-second lease; workers renew the lease every 10 seconds; an expired lease makes the job available again; handlers must be idempotent because a job can run twice; only explicit acknowledgement removes a job. acceptance.answerPlacement: Opens with a substantive explanation of queue behavior, without announcing the explanation.
acceptance.actionableSteps: Explains the renewal/expiry/idempotency/acknowledgement relationship usefully; does not invent operational tasks.
acceptance.completeness: Covers all seven facts and why each matters, with no dashboard tangent or invented exactly-once guarantee.

responses.text:
The queue uses renewable leases to make unfinished jobs available again, and explicit acknowledgement to remove them. Handlers must tolerate duplicate runs.

1. **Capacity is 100 jobs.** This bounds how many jobs the queue can hold.
2. **Jobs beyond capacity are rejected.** Rejection makes failed admission visible instead of silently losing jobs.
3. **A running job has a 30-second lease.** The lease limits how long it can remain leased without renewal.
4. **Workers renew every 10 seconds.** Renewal keeps the lease active while work continues, with renewal scheduled before its 30-second expiry.
5. **An expired lease makes the job available again.** This allows another attempt when the current worker stops renewing.
6. **Handlers must be idempotent because a job can run twice.** Repeating a job must not produce an additional unintended effect.
7. **Only explicit acknowledgement removes a job.** Running a handler or renewing its lease does not remove the job.

Renewal keeps a running job leased. If renewal stops and the lease expires, the job becomes available again—even if the earlier attempt already produced an effect. That creates the possibility of duplicate runs, which idempotent handlers must handle. Explicit acknowledgement is the removal step; lease expiry is a retry opportunity, not removal.
